items.q: A server suddenly becomes slow: which commands do you run in the first 60 seconds?
items.a:
Netflix's checklist is deliberately ordered — each command rules out a category of causes: 
uptime                  # 1/5/15-minute load averages — is the trend rising or falling?
dmesg | tail            # OOM killer? hardware errors? packet drops?
vmstat 1                # r (run queue), si/so (swap), us/sy/id/wa
mpstat -P ALL 1         # one stuck core or the entire machine? (single-thread bottleneck)
pidstat 1               # which process is consuming CPU, steadily or in bursts?
iostat -xz 1            # %util, await — is disk the bottleneck?
free -m                 # how much RAM remains, and how much is in buff/cache?
sar -n DEV 1            # has network bandwidth reached its ceiling?
sar -n TCP,ETCP 1       # retransmits and connection errors
top                     # one final overall view
The idea: within one minute, you know whether the bottleneck is in [[o:CPU, memory, disk, or the network]] — only then do you drill down in that direction. :::tip Interview answer You do not need to memorize all ten commands. Articulate the [[g:diagnostic framework]] — *"I first narrow it down to CPU / RAM / disk / network, then move into the JVM"* — and add 3–4 concrete commands; that is convincing enough. ::: :::deep - [[r:The biggest trap]]: jumping straight into the application when the cause lies in a lower layer (full disk, slow DNS, NTP drift, or a CPU-throttled container). - inside a [[o:container]], `top`/`free` often report **host** metrics rather than cgroup metrics → read `/sys/fs/cgroup/...` (`memory.max`, `cpu.stat`). A rising `nr_throttled` means CPU throttling — a symptom commonly misdiagnosed as 'the app is slow'. - `df -h` and `df -i`: a full disk [[r:and]] inode exhaustion both make applications fail in confusing ways; `df -i` is easy to forget - check time synchronization with `chronyc tracking` — clock drift breaks tokens, signatures, and every time-based calculation - modern tools such as `bpftop`, `execsnoop`, and `biolatency` (bcc/BPF) expose syscalls and per-process I/O latency without stopping anything - always compare against [[g:a baseline]]: 'load 8' is meaningless unless you know the normal value and the machine's core count :::

items.q: How should you interpret load average, iowait, and CPU steal?
items.a:
**Load average** — on Linux, it is [[r:not]] merely the "number of processes waiting for CPU." Linux also counts processes in the [[b:D]] state (uninterruptible sleep — usually waiting on disk or NFS). The consequence: [[o:high load with idle CPU]] means an I/O bottleneck, not a CPU shortage. This is a very common misreading. It only becomes meaningful relative to the core count: a load of 8 on a 16-core machine is comfortable; on a 2-core machine, it is overloaded. Compare the 1/5/15-minute values to see whether the trend is [[g:rising or falling]]. **Reading `vmstat 1`:** 
procs -----------memory---------- ---swap-- -----io---- --system-- ------cpu-----
 r  b   swpd   free   buff  cache   si   so    bi    bo   in   cs us sy id wa st
 9  2      0 128360  22140 918224    0    0    12   840 4210 8830 71 12  5 10  2
- [[b:r]] — tasks waiting for CPU. If it remains above the core count, the machine genuinely lacks CPU capacity. - [[b:b]] — tasks blocked on I/O - [[b:si/so]] — swap in/out. Any nonzero value is a [[r:red flag]] for a latency-sensitive service. - [[b:wa]] (iowait) — the CPU is idle *while* I/O remains pending - [[b:st]] (steal) — the hypervisor has taken CPU time to run another VM :::warn High iowait is not necessarily a problem `wa` says only, *"the CPU is idle and some I/O is waiting."* High `wa` is normal on a machine running disk-heavy batch jobs. Conversely, `wa` = 0 does [[r:not]] mean the disk is healthy — if the CPU is 100% busy, time spent waiting for I/O is not counted in `wa`. ::: :::deep - [[o:steal time]] (`st`) is a cloud-specific gotcha: when a shared instance (T-series burstable) exhausts its credits, `st` spikes and the application slows down while every internal metric looks 'normal'. On EC2 T2/T3, also inspect `CPUCreditBalance`. Calling this out is a strong signal of production experience. - abnormally high context switches (`cs`) indicate too many threads or severe lock contention → correlate with a thread dump (21-linux-production-debug.jvm-network-deep-dive-on-prod.q1) - `%util` from `iostat` is [[r:misleading]] for SSDs/NVMe: they process many I/Os concurrently, so 100% `%util` does not necessarily mean saturation. Inspect [[g:`await` and `aqu-sz`]] instead of `%util`. - for Java services, swap should usually be [[o:disabled entirely]] (`swappiness=0` or no swap allocation) — GC scans the entire heap, and a heap paged out to disk turns pauses into multi-second events. K8s disables swap by default for exactly this reason. - pressure stall information (`/proc/pressure/{cpu,io,memory}`) is a modern signal that is far more interpretable than load average — mentioning it shows current operational knowledge :::

items.q: Running out of file descriptors or ephemeral ports: what are the symptoms and fixes?
items.a:
These are two different failures with the same symptom: a service runs normally for hours, then [[r:suddenly cannot accept or open any connections]]. **File descriptor exhaustion** 
java.net.SocketException: Too many open files
Every socket, file, and pipe consumes an fd. 
ulimit -n                          # soft limit for the current shell
cat /proc/<pid>/limits             # ACTUAL limit for the running process
ls /proc/<pid>/fd | wc -l          # number currently in use
lsof -p <pid> | awk '{print $5}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
The cause is almost always [[o:a leak]]: an `HttpClient`/`InputStream`/`Connection` that is never closed. Raising `ulimit` merely postpones the crash — you still have to find the leak. **Ephemeral port exhaustion** 
java.net.BindException: Cannot assign requested address
The client opens too many outbound connections. The default range, `32768–60999`, provides approximately 28,000 ports for each (destination IP, destination port) pair. 
ss -s                                        # overview, including the TIME-WAIT count
cat /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_local_port_range
ss -tan state time-wait | wc -l
The usual culprit is [[r:creating a new client for every request]] instead of reusing a connection pool. Each closed connection remains in `TIME_WAIT` for 60 seconds. :::deep - systemd [[r:ignores]] `/etc/security/limits.conf`; set `LimitNOFILE=` in the unit file instead. This explains the classic 'I already raised ulimit, but it still fails' incident. - in K8s, the fd limit comes from the image/runtime, not your shell — inspect `/proc/1/limits` inside the container - [[g:The root fix]] for ephemeral port exhaustion is connection pooling plus keep-alive. Share one `WebClient`/`HttpClient` across the application, not one per call. - `TIME_WAIT` is [[o:intentional]]: it allows delayed packets from an old connection to expire. `tcp_tw_reuse=1` is safe on the **client** side; `tcp_tw_recycle` was removed from the kernel because it breaks NAT — proposing it as a 'solution' is a red flag. - distinguish them quickly: `Too many open files` = the local process exhausted its fds; `Cannot assign requested address` = source ports are exhausted; `Connection refused` = nothing is listening remotely; `Connection reset` = the peer closed abruptly - monitor proactively: export `process.files.open` / `process.files.max` to Prometheus and alert at 80% — this class of incident is entirely predictable :::

items.q: The OOM killer terminated a service: how do you trace the cause and prevent it?
items.a:
There are two completely different kinds of OOM; [[r:do not confuse them]]:
Java OutOfMemoryErrorLinux OOM killer
Who terminates itthe JVM throws an exceptionthe kernel sends SIGKILL
Evidencea stack trace in the application lognothing in the application log
Where to lookapplication logsdmesg, /var/log/syslog
Causeinsufficient heap / a leaktotal RSS exceeds the machine or cgroup limit
dmesg -T | grep -i -E "oom|killed process"
# Out of memory: Killed process 4127 (java) total-vm:9863244kB, anon-rss:6291456kB
In K8s, an OOM-terminated container is reported as `OOMKilled` with exit code [[b:137]] (128 + 9). **Why OOM can still occur when `-Xmx` is lower than RAM:** the heap is [[o:not]] the JVM's entire memory footprint. There is also metaspace, the code cache, thread stacks (~1MB/thread), direct ByteBuffers, and native-library memory. 
RSS ≈ Heap + Metaspace + CodeCache + (Threads × Stack) + Direct + Native
A practical rule is to set `-Xmx` to approximately [[g:50–70%]] of the container limit, not 90%. :::deep - Java 10+ [[g:automatically detects the cgroup limit]] (`UseContainerSupport` is enabled by default). Prefer `-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=70` over a fixed `-Xmx` — resizing the container then requires no flag change. - older Java 8 releases [[r:do not recognize]] cgroups: the JVM sees all host RAM and sets its default heap to one quarter of that value → immediate OOMKilled. This is a classic failure when containerizing an old Java application. - use [[o:Native Memory Tracking]] to investigate memory outside the heap: `-XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary`, then `jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory summary` - common off-heap leaks include direct ByteBuffers that are not released (Netty), thread pools that create unbounded numbers of threads, and `ZipInputStream`/native libraries that are not closed - always enable `-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError -XX:HeapDumpPath=/dump` — [[g:without a dump, there is nothing to investigate]] (21-linux-production-debug.jvm-network-deep-dive-on-prod.q2). Remember to mount a volume; a dump written to the container's ephemeral filesystem disappears with the container. - in K8s, set `requests` = `limits` for critical services (QoS Guaranteed) so they are not killed first when a node runs short of memory; `oom_score_adj` determines which process dies first - OOMKilled recurring at regular intervals indicates [[o:a leak]]; occurring specifically at peak load indicates [[o:underprovisioning]]. These are different conclusions with different fixes. :::

items.q: How do you read a thread dump to find deadlocks and blocked threads?
items.a:
jcmd <pid> Thread.print > td1.txt     # recommended approach
jstack -l <pid> > td1.txt            # equivalent; -l adds lock information
Take [[g:three dumps 5–10 seconds apart]] — a single snapshot cannot distinguish "running" from "stuck." A thread whose stack remains unchanged across all three is the likely culprit. **States to recognize:**
StateMeaningConcerning when
RUNNABLErunning (or waiting on network I/O)many threads are stopped at the same line of compute code
BLOCKEDwaiting to enter synchronizedmany threads are waiting on the same monitor
WAITINGwait() or park() with no timeouta thread waits indefinitely because nothing wakes it
TIMED_WAITINGhas a timeoutusually normal
**Deadlock** — the JVM detects it automatically and prints it explicitly at the end of the dump: 
Found one Java-level deadlock:
=============================
"thread-A": waiting to lock monitor 0x00007f8 (object 0x000000076ab, a java.lang.Object),
  which is held by "thread-B"
"thread-B": waiting to lock monitor 0x00007f9 (object 0x000000076ac, a java.lang.Object),
  which is held by "thread-A"
:::warn Common misreading A `RUNNABLE` thread at `socketRead0` is [[r:not]] consuming CPU — it is waiting on the network. The JVM cannot distinguish blocking I/O from computation here. Many `RUNNABLE` threads at `socketRead0` mean an external dependency is slow, not that the application is CPU-bound. ::: :::deep - The most important pattern to recognize is [[o:dozens of `BLOCKED` threads on the same monitor]] → a contention bottleneck. Inspect the `- locked <0x...>` line to identify the owning thread, then read **its** stack — that is the code path you need to fix. - pool exhaustion is immediately visible in a dump: many `TIMED_WAITING` threads at `HikariPool.getConnection` → this is not a database failure; connections are being held too long elsewhere (18-query-optimization.rewriting-the-query-reshaping-the-model.q4) - `jcmd` is [[g:safer than]] `jstack` (no `-F` required and less risk of hanging the JVM). Forced `jstack -F` can pause the JVM for a long time — use it sparingly in production. - meaningful thread names (`booking-worker-3`) make a dump far easier to read than `pool-2-thread-7`. Name every custom thread pool. - deadlocks involving `ReentrantLock` are [[r:not]] always detected by the JVM as `synchronized` deadlocks are — use `jstack -l` to see `Locked ownable synchronizers` - analysis tools include fastThread.io, or use `jstack | grep -A3 "java.lang.Thread.State" | sort | uniq -c` for a quick count by state - virtual threads (23-java-concurrency-coding.async-the-modern-toolkit.q4) change the workflow: use `jcmd <pid> Thread.dump_to_file -format=json` to capture them all :::

items.q: How do you use a heap dump to find the source of a memory leak?
items.a:
**Recognize the leak before taking a dump:** graph heap usage after each Full GC. Normal behavior is a sawtooth around a stable baseline; a leak produces [[r:a steadily rising sawtooth floor]] that eventually ends in OOM. 
jcmd <pid> GC.heap_info                      # quick overview
jcmd <pid> GC.class_histogram | head -30     # low overhead and often enough for an initial diagnosis
jcmd <pid> GC.heap_dump /dump/heap.hprof     # full dump
:::warn Heap dumps can pause the JVM `GC.heap_dump` causes a [[r:stop-the-world]] pause proportional to heap size — dumping an 8GB heap can stall the process for tens of seconds. In production, drain the instance from the load balancer first, or dump an instance that is leaking but is not serving traffic. ::: **Analyze it with Eclipse MAT** — use these three views in order: 1. [[g:Leak Suspects Report]] — MAT identifies likely suspects automatically and is correct in most cases 2. [[g:Dominator Tree]] — sort by *retained heap* (memory that would be released if this object died), not *shallow heap* 3. [[g:Path to GC Roots]] (exclude weak/soft references) — answers the most important question: [[o:what is retaining it]] **Classic Java leak patterns:** - a `static` Map/List used as a cache [[r:with no bound and no TTL]] - a registered listener/callback that is never unregistered - a `ThreadLocal` without `remove()` — pool threads live forever, so their values do too - a `ClassLoader` leak during hot redeployment (a classic Tomcat problem) - a `HashMap` key that does not implement `equals`/`hashCode` → prior entries are never found again and only accumulate :::deep - Distinguish [[o:shallow]] size (the object itself) from [[o:retained]] size (the entire object graph kept alive exclusively by it). Sorting by shallow size almost always leads to `char[]`/`byte[]` — correct but useless. - seeing `char[]`/`byte[]` at the top of the histogram is [[r:normal]]; the real questions are *which strings* and *what retains them* — only Path to GC Roots can answer those - compare [[g:two dumps taken a few hours apart]] (MAT can compare histograms) — growing objects are the suspects; objects that were already large are often innocent - with an [[o:off-heap]] leak, the heap dump looks completely clean while RSS keeps growing → switch to Native Memory Tracking (21-linux-production-debug.diagnosing-the-system.q4) - continuous JFR recording lets you investigate *after* an incident without reproducing it: `-XX:StartFlightRecording=disk=true,maxsize=1g,dumponexit=true` - a dump contains [[r:all live data]] held in memory — passwords, tokens, and customer information. Treat the `.hprof` file as sensitive data: encrypt it, restrict access, and delete it after analysis. :::

items.q: How safe are async-profiler and JFR for profiling in production?
items.a:
The underlying question is: *are you willing to measure in production, and do you know how to do it without making the incident worse?* **async-profiler** — a tool worth knowing by name: 
./profiler.sh -d 30 -e cpu -f /tmp/cpu.html <pid>      # 30s CPU profile, output as a flame graph
./profiler.sh -d 30 -e alloc -f /tmp/alloc.html <pid>  # highest-allocation sites
./profiler.sh -d 30 -e lock -f /tmp/lock.html <pid>    # lock contention
Overhead is [[g:~1–3%]] at the default sampling frequency — low enough for production use. It uses `AsyncGetCallTrace` plus perf events, so it has [[o:no safepoint bias]] — the issue that makes older sampling profilers (VisualVM and JProfiler in sampling mode) collect samples only at safepoints and [[r:report the wrong hotspots]]. Understanding this distinction is a strong signal of production profiling experience. **JFR** — built into the JDK, with nothing extra to install: 
jcmd <pid> JFR.start name=diag settings=profile duration=60s filename=/tmp/r.jfr
jcmd <pid> JFR.dump name=diag filename=/tmp/r.jfr
Open the recording in JDK Mission Control. JFR covers more than async-profiler — GC, I/O, exceptions, threads, locks, and allocations — but async-profiler presents CPU flame graphs more clearly. **Reading a flame graph:** the horizontal axis is the [[o:share of time]] (not elapsed time), and the vertical axis is stack depth. Look for [[g:wide plateaus]] — functions that account for many samples. Tall, narrow spikes are not concerning; broad, flat areas are where the cost lies. :::deep - if a CPU profile does not explain why the application is slow, the bottleneck is [[r:not CPU]]. Switch to `-e wall` (wall-clock) to include time waiting on I/O and locks — misreading this is the most common mistake. - `-e alloc` reveals allocation pressure: reducing garbage often improves p99 more than optimizing an algorithm because it lowers GC frequency - async-profiler needs an appropriate `perf_event_paranoid` setting and often `SYS_ADMIN`/`--cap-add` inside a container; JFR requires no special privileges — in a locked-down K8s environment, JFR is often the only option - [[g:always-on JFR]] (`disk=true, maxage=6h`) is well worth enabling by default: when an incident occurs, the data already exists and you do not have to wait for a reproduction - always capture a normal [[o:baseline]] for comparison — a single flame graph says 'this code is expensive,' not 'this code is *unusually* expensive' - `-XX:+DebugNonSafepoints` makes stacks much more accurate after JIT inlining (nearly essential when profiling hot code) - Java 21+: JFR includes virtual-thread events (pinning, submit failed) — exactly what you need when debugging 23.8 :::

items.q: How do tcpdump, ss, and netstat help debug networking between two services?
items.a:
When two services "cannot talk to each other," you need to determine where the packets stop. **Check the connection first:** 
ss -tanp | grep :5432          # connections to Postgres, including the process
ss -tan state syn-sent         # SYN sent with no reply => blocked by firewall/SG
ss -ti dst 10.0.3.41           # RTT, cwnd, and retransmits for each connection
`ss` [[g:replaces `netstat`]] and is much faster on hosts with many connections — using `netstat` today signals outdated operational knowledge. **Capture packets when you need definitive evidence:** 
tcpdump -i any -nn 'host 10.0.3.41 and port 5432' -c 200 -w /tmp/c.pcap
tcpdump -nn -r /tmp/c.pcap | head -40
`-nn`, which disables DNS and port-name resolution, is [[o:important]]: resolution can hang the command when DNS itself is the problem. **Reading the result:** - repeated `SYN` packets with no `SYN-ACK` → traffic is [[r:being blocked]] (security group, NACL, or iptables), or the destination does not exist - `SYN` → immediate `RST` → [[r:nothing is listening]] on that port - the handshake completes, followed by a long silence → the peer received the request but is processing it slowly (an application problem, not a network problem) - `[R]` partway through → the peer closed abruptly, often because of an LB timeout or idle timeout :::deep - symptoms can distinguish these cases faster than a packet capture: [[o:hanging until the timeout]] means packets are being swallowed (firewall DROP); an [[o:immediate failure]] means an RST or ICMP-unreachable response arrived - `ss -s` shows total connections and `TIME-WAIT` (see 21.3); `ss -ti` shows `retrans` — high retransmissions mean there is a genuine network problem - [[r:The MTU trap]]: the connection opens and small requests succeed, but large requests hang → packet fragmentation or PMTU discovery is broken because ICMP is blocked. This is common with VPNs and K8s overlay networks, and very hard to recognize until you have seen it once. - in K8s, use `kubectl debug`/an ephemeral container to run `tcpdump` in the same network namespace without adding diagnostic tools to the production image - DNS: run `dig +short svc.ns.svc.cluster.local` and inspect `ndots:5` in `/etc/resolv.conf` — this setting can make each external-name lookup try 4–5 suffixes and is a common cause of 'mysterious slowness' on K8s - TLS payloads are encrypted, so `tcpdump` shows only the handshake — diagnose certificate/SNI issues with `openssl s_client -connect host:443 -servername host` - [[r:A pcap file contains real traffic data]]. Limit the capture with `-c`, use a narrow filter, and delete it after analysis. :::
